bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Adding at the millisecond level delegates every hard calendar question — month ends, leap days (note 2024-03-01 minus a day is Feb 29), year rollovers — to the Date engine. Hand-incrementing the day-of-month field is how the classic "Jan 32nd" bugs are born.
hints: getTime() + days * 86400000, wrap in new Date, format with toISOString().slice(0, 10).

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `earliest` that takes an array of ISO date strings and returns the earliest one (the original string). Assume non-empty input.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Comparing through `getTime()` is explicit and always correct. (Full ISO-with-Z strings of the same format also sort correctly as plain strings — a useful property of the format — but converting to numbers states the intent and survives mixed formats.)
hints: Track the best-so-far string; compare via getTime().

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `dayName` that takes an ISO date string and returns the English UTC weekday name (`'Sunday'` ... `'Saturday'`). `'2024-03-15T00:00:00Z'` is a Friday.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Same lookup-table shape as monthName, with the crucial detail that `getUTCDay()` numbers from Sunday, not Monday — put Monday first in the array and every label shifts by one day, a bug that looks right six days a week in testing.
hints: A 7-element lookup array indexed by getUTCDay() — remember it starts at Sunday.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `lastDayOfMonth` that takes an ISO date string and returns the number of days in that UTC month, e.g. February 2024 → `29` (leap year). Hint: `Date.UTC(year, month + 1, 0)` is the timestamp of the LAST day of `month`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `Date.UTC(y, m + 1, 0)` exploits Date's field normalization: day 0 is 'one before day 1', i.e. the last day of the previous month. The engine handles 28/29/30/31 and leap years — encoding those rules yourself is a rite of passage nobody needs.
hints: Day 0 of NEXT month rolls back to the final day of this one; read it with getUTCDate().

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `formatLong(iso)` returning `'<MonthName> <day>, <year>'` using UTC values — e.g. `'2024-03-05T00:00:00Z'` → `'March 5, 2024'` (day without leading zero).
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `getUTCDate()` returns a plain number, so "5" needs no de-padding — unlike slicing it from the ISO string, which would give "05". Choosing getters vs string slicing depends on the target format: machine formats slice the ISO string; human formats use the numeric getters.
hints: Month lookup table + getUTCDate() (already unpadded) + getUTCFullYear() in one template literal.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `quarterOf(iso)` returning the calendar quarter 1-4 of the UTC month: Jan-Mar → 1, Apr-Jun → 2, Jul-Sep → 3, Oct-Dec → 4.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The arithmetic trick: 0-indexed months divide evenly into quarters with `Math.floor(month / 3)`, giving 0-3, then `+ 1` humanizes it. The boundary tests (Mar 31 vs Apr 1, Sep 30 vs Oct 1) pin the edges where off-by-one bugs live.
hints: Months 0-2 are Q1, 3-5 Q2... integer-divide the 0-indexed month by 3, then + 1.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `sortDatesAsc(isoDates)` returning a NEW array of the ISO strings sorted earliest-first (do not mutate the input). Compare via `getTime()`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Two habits combine here: copy-before-sort (because `Array.prototype.sort` mutates, and the caller’s array is not yours to reorder) and the numeric comparator over `getTime()`. Sorting timelines — posts, events, messages — is this exact function with different field access.
hints: Copy first (`[...arr]`) — sort mutates in place.
The comparator subtracts timestamps: negative means a comes first.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `ageInDays(createdIso, nowIso)` returning how many whole days old a record is — `Math.floor` of the millisecond difference divided by 86400000. A record created 36 hours ago is 1 day old.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The rounding mode is the design decision: `floor` means "completed days only", so 36 hours is 1 day and 23 hours is 0 — matching how people read "N days old". `round` would call 36 hours "2 days". Pick floor/round/ceil deliberately per use case; they differ on every partial day.
hints: Same subtraction as daysBetween, but Math.floor — partial days don’t count toward age.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions:
Export `dueStatus(dueIso, nowIso)` comparing a task's due date to an injected "now" (both full ISO strings with Z). Compute the whole-day difference (due minus now, via getTime and 86400000, Math.round) and return:
- `'overdue'` when the difference is negative
- `'due-today'` when it is 0
- `'due-soon'` when it is 1 to 3 days
- `'ok'` for anything later
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Injecting `nowIso` is what makes a time-dependent feature testable: the tests freeze "now" at a chosen instant and every boundary can be pinned exactly. The function decomposes into the two skills of this lesson — millisecond subtraction for the difference, then an ordered threshold ladder for classification. In the real app, only the outermost caller touches the actual clock: `dueStatus(task.due, new Date().toISOString())`.
hints: First compute diffDays exactly like daysBetween; then it is a pure classification problem.
Order the branches from most negative to most positive — each check can then be a simple threshold.
The 3/4 day boundary: 3 is still due-soon, 4 is ok.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: What does `/\d+/.test("abc")` return?
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `.test` is the yes/no method: a boolean, nothing more. `"abc"` contains no digit, so false. When you only need existence, prefer `test` over `match` — no null-handling required.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Why does `/\d+/.test("item42")` return `true`, and how do you make a pattern that only accepts ALL-digit strings?
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: A regex scans for its pattern *anywhere* unless told otherwise — "item42" contains the digit run "42", so the unanchored test passes. `^` pins the match to the start and `$` to the end, leaving no room for other characters. Forgotten anchors are the top validation-regex bug.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: What does `'hello'.match(/\d+/)` return?
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `match` returns `null` on no match, not an empty array — so `s.match(re)[0]` is a TypeError waiting for the first non-matching input. Either check the result first or use optional chaining: `s.match(re)?.[0]`.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: What is the difference between `'a1b2'.replace(/\d/, '#')` and `'a1b2'.replace(/\d/g, '#')`?
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `replace` with a non-global regex stops after one substitution — a notorious silent bug since the code works perfectly on single-occurrence test data. The `g` flag means 'all occurrences'. (For plain strings, `replaceAll` is the modern alternative.)

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Why does `/v1.2/.test("v132")` return `true`, and what pattern tests for the literal text "v1.2"?
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The dot is a wildcard — `v1.2` means 'v1, any character, 2', which 'v132' satisfies. `\.` turns it back into a literal period. Dots in version numbers, filenames, and domains are the most common place this wildcard silently over-matches.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: No digit in 'abc' (false); one in 'a1c' (true). 'catalog' starts with 'cat' so the start-anchored test passes, but with both anchors the whole string must BE 'cat' — false. The global match collects every digit run: '9' and '88'.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The full match occupies index 0, then each capture group in left-to-right order: the four-digit year "2024", then the digit run "0042". `Number("0042")` strips the leading zeros → 42. Capture groups are how regex goes from "does it match" to "pull the pieces out".
hints: m[0] is the entire match; m[1] and m[2] are the parenthesized groups in order. \d{4} is exactly four digits.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `hasDigit` that returns `true` when the string contains at least one digit.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `test` with an unanchored single `\d` asks exactly "is there a digit anywhere?" — password rules, input heuristics, and validators compose from tiny checks like this.
hints: One \d, no anchors — "contains" is the unanchored default.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `isDigitsOnly` that returns `true` when the string is non-empty and consists ONLY of digits.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The three pieces each earn their place: `^`/`$` forbid any non-digit sneaking in at the edges, and `+` (rather than `*`) requires at least one digit, rejecting the empty string. This is the pattern for ids arriving as URL path segments.
hints: Anchor both ends and use + (one or more) so the empty string fails.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `extractDigits` that returns all digits of the string concatenated, e.g. `'a1b22c'` → `'122'`, and `''` when there are none.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The global match collects every digit, and the null-guard turns "no match" into the sensible empty string. Normalizing phone numbers (the third case) is this function’s day job. An equivalent: `s.replace(/\D/g, "")` — delete all NON-digits.
hints: match(/\d/g) gives an array of single digits — or null, which you must handle.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `isEmailish` that loosely validates an email with ONE regex: one or more non-space/non-@ characters, then `@`, then more such characters, a literal dot, and more such characters. Use the pattern `/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Reading the pattern: `[^\s@]+` = a run of characters that are neither whitespace nor `@`; the escaped `\.` is a literal dot (unescaped `.` matches anything). This deliberately loose shape — something@something.something — is what practical forms use; real validation is clicking the confirmation link.
hints: [^\s@] is a negated character class: any char EXCEPT whitespace and @. The dot must be escaped: \.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `idFromSlug` that extracts the trailing numeric id from a slug as a NUMBER: `'post-123'` → `123`. Return `null` when the slug does not end in digits.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The `$` anchor is what rejects 'v2-intro' — it has digits, but not at the end. Capture + convert + null-on-miss is the complete extraction idiom: routing layers pull entity ids out of URLs exactly this way.
hints: Capture (\d+) anchored to the end with $; convert m[1] with Number.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `maskDigits` that replaces every digit with `'*'`, e.g. `'card 1234'` → `'card ****'`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Without `g`, only the 1 in "1234" would be masked — the classic partial-redaction bug, dangerous precisely because the output still looks redacted. Regex `replace` shines where plain `replaceAll` cannot: the thing being replaced is a *pattern*, not a fixed string.
hints: replace with /\d/g — the g flag is the whole exercise.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `normalizeSpaces` that collapses every run of whitespace to a single space and trims the ends: `'  a   b  '` → `'a b'`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: `\s` covers tabs and newlines too — which `replaceAll("  ", " ")` never could, and `+` collapses a whole run in one replacement. Cleaning pasted user input before storage is the canonical use.
hints: \s+ matches a run of ANY whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines); replace with one space, then trim.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `countWords` that returns the number of words in the string, where words are runs of non-whitespace. The empty or all-whitespace string has 0 words.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Matching the words (`\S+` globally) and counting beats splitting on spaces, which produces phantom empty strings for leading/trailing/double whitespace. The capital-letter negations (`\S`, `\D`) read as "anything but".
hints: \S (capital) is the opposite of \s: non-whitespace. Match globally, count the array.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `startsWithUpper` that returns `true` when the string starts with an uppercase letter A-Z.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: A `^` anchor plus a character range checks exactly one position — the first. Note the empty string: with nothing at position 0 the pattern cannot match, so no special guard is needed; the regex handles the edge case naturally.
hints: Anchor to the start with ^ and use the character range [A-Z].

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `extractHashtags` that returns an array of all hashtags in the text WITHOUT their `#`, e.g. `'love #js and #regex'` → `['js', 'regex']`, and `[]` when there are none. A hashtag is `#` followed by one or more letters/digits (pattern `/#([a-z0-9]+)/g` on lowercase input; assume lowercase).
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: With the `g` flag, `match` returns whole matches only (groups are dropped), so the pragmatic move is matching `#tag` and slicing the prefix off. The null-to-empty-array normalization at the end means callers can always `.map` the result.
hints: Global match keeps the # — strip it afterwards with slice(1). (matchAll gives groups directly, but match+slice is simpler here.)

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export a function `stripNonAlnum` that removes every character that is not a letter or digit, e.g. `'he!!o, w0rld?'` → `'heow0rld'`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Deleting with a negated class — "replace everything that is NOT allowed with nothing" — is often simpler than keeping what is allowed. The `g` flag again: without it, only the first `!` would vanish.
hints: A negated class [^a-zA-Z0-9] matches the characters you want GONE; replace them with the empty string.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `isValidSlug(s)` returning `true` when `s` consists only of lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens, does not start or end with a hyphen, and is non-empty. Suggested pattern: `/^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Instead of listing the forbidden placements of hyphens, the pattern describes the legal *structure* — `segment(-segment)*` — and every hyphen rule falls out for free: no leading (the string must start with a segment), no trailing or doubled (each hyphen must be followed by a segment). Describing valid structure usually beats patching exceptions.
hints: Think in segments: one alphanumeric run, then zero or more (hyphen + run) groups.
The segment structure automatically forbids leading, trailing, and doubled hyphens.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `swapNameOrder(s)` converting `'Last, First'` to `'First Last'` using `replace` with capture groups: pattern `/^(\w+), (\w+)$/` and replacement `'$2 $1'`. Return the input unchanged when it doesn't match the pattern.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: Capture groups work in replacements too: `$1`/`$2` splice the captured pieces into a new arrangement — a one-line reformat that would otherwise take split/trim/join gymnastics. And `replace` on a non-matching string is a no-op, which handles the fallback case for free.
hints: In a replacement string, $1 and $2 refer to the capture groups.
replace returns the string unchanged when the pattern does not match — no guard needed.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions: Export `redactEmails(text)` replacing every email-looking token (pattern `/[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+/g`) with `'[email]'`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: The same pattern serves validation and redaction with two adjustments: anchors come OFF (we are hunting inside text now, not checking a whole string) and `g` goes ON (all occurrences). Knowing when a pattern needs anchors is half of practical regex.
hints: Reuse the loose email pattern from isEmailish — minus the anchors, plus the g flag.

bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.instructions:
Export `parseRoute(path)` for URL paths shaped like `'/posts/123'` or `'/users/7/comments'`. Match with the pattern `/^\/([a-z]+)\/(\d+)(?:\/([a-z]+))?$/` (or equivalent) and return:
- `{ resource, id, sub }` — resource as string, id as NUMBER, sub as string or `null` when the third segment is absent
- `null` when the path does not match at all
E.g. `'/posts/123'` → `{ resource: 'posts', id: 123, sub: null }`; `'/users/7/comments'` → `{ resource: 'users', id: 7, sub: 'comments' }`.
bootforge/errors-modules/modules-and-dat.explanation: This is a toy version of what every web router does: one anchored pattern both *validates* the path shape and *extracts* its parts. The two regex features doing the heavy lifting: `(?: ... )` groups without capturing (so the optional slash doesn’t pollute the captures), and `?` makes that whole group optional — with an unparticipating group yielding `undefined`, normalized to `null` at the boundary. Anchors reject partial matches like `'posts/123'` missing its leading slash.
hints: Slashes inside the pattern must be escaped: \/ . The (?: ... )? wrapper makes the whole third segment optional without capturing the slash.
When the optional group did not participate, its capture is undefined — convert to null with ?? null.
Convert the id capture with Number().
